content.title: About
content.content: Banana chips are thinly sliced and dried banana pieces, usually fried or baked until crisp. They have a sweet, slightly caramelized flavor and can be seasoned salty or sweet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Banana chips are often used as a healthier alternative to potato chips.
They can be prepared by deep‑frying, oven‑baking, or freeze‑drying.
Sweet banana chips are sometimes coated with chocolate, nuts, or spices such as cinnamon.
Bananas chosen for chips are typically ripe but not over‑ripe to retain natural sweetness.
In countries like the Philippines and Indonesia, banana chips are a traditional snack.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Bananas provide a high amount of potassium, which supports heart and muscle function.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Banana chips retain some antioxidants such as dopamine and vitamin C that combat free radicals.

items.title: Quick energy snack
items.content: Carbohydrates provide a fast source of energy, useful for travel or active pursuits.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions may contain added sugar, which is unsuitable for diabetes or low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Oil‑fried chips can be calorie‑rich, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Banana allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to bananas, experiencing symptoms from mild rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salted varieties often contain added sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Banana chips are convenient as a standalone snack, added to granola, yogurt, salads, or used in baking. Lightly sprinkle with spices—cinnamon, paprika, or cocoa—for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Black beans are cooked Phaseolus vulgaris beans canned in their own juice or a low‑sodium brine (2131 mg Na per 100 g). They have a soft, slightly sweet texture and a rich earthy flavor. Commonly used in Mexican, South American, and Caribbean cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans are rich in antioxidants, especially anthocyanins that give them their dark color.
In Latin American cuisine they are called “frijoles negros” and appear in dishes like feijoada and black bean soup.
Canned beans can be stored at room temperature for up to 3 years.
Reduced‑sodium versions are better suited for people monitoring their salt intake.
They provide a good source of plant protein and dietary fiber.

items.title: High in plant protein
items.content: One cup of canned black beans delivers about 15 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These nutrients are essential for blood formation and preventing anemia, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: The reduced salt content makes the product safer for individuals with hypertension or cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and other polyphenols combat free radicals, supporting cellular health.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; pairing beans with vitamin C‑rich foods helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals; increase intake gradually.

items.title: Carbohydrate content
items.content: Although they have a low glycemic index, beans still contain carbs, which should be considered on strict low‑carb diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add black beans to salads, soups, chili, tacos, rice dishes, and vegetarian patties. They are also used as fillings for burritos or as a side dish. Before use, shake the can and drain the brine if you want even less sodium.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer beans to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 5 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

double-hamburger-on-white-bun-2-medium-p.title: Double hamburger on white bun, 2 medium patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double hamburger consists of two medium beef patties (about 100 g each) placed between a split white bun. It is usually topped with lettuce, tomato slice, pickles, onion, cheese, sauce and seasonings. This classic fast‑food item is popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first double hamburger appeared in the United States in the 1930s as a “two‑in‑one” variant.
White buns typically contain more sugar and fat than whole‑grain buns, giving them a softer, sweeter texture.
A 100 g patty is considered “medium” in the fast‑food industry; two such patties provide roughly 200 g of meat.
The combination of two patties and sauce raises the calorie count to 600–800 kcal depending on toppings.
In some countries the double hamburger is served without cheese to highlight the beef flavor.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Two beef patties deliver about 40 g of protein, essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef provides vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Calcium (when cheese is added)
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A double hamburger can contain 600–800 kcal, which may contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fat and cholesterol
items.content: Beef and cheese contain saturated fats that, in excess, can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and pickles add a significant amount of sodium, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The white bun is made from wheat, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef patties may harbor pathogenic bacteria such as E. coli.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burger is typically eaten by hand, holding it by the bun. Additional sauce can be added, the bun can be swapped for a whole‑grain version, or cheese can be omitted to reduce calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A prepared burger can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze it and reheat in an oven or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: White fish, mixed species, steamed, is a tender and low‑fat source of protein. Steaming preserves the natural flavor, moisture, and most nutrients, making the dish light and nutritious.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The white fish mix usually includes cod, haddock, pollock and sea bass.
Steaming retains up to 90 % of B‑vitamins that are often lost during frying.
White fish is low in fat but rich in omega‑3 fatty acids beneficial for heart health.
Steamed fish is a traditional dish in Scandinavian and Asian cuisines.
Steam cooking reduces the formation of harmful compounds that can appear when frying at high temperatures.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Steamed fish contains less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Contains EPA and DHA, which support cardiovascular health and brain function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: High in B12, niacin and B6, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides selenium, iodine and phosphorus, which aid thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain fish species can accumulate mercury and other toxins; varying fish sources is recommended.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When salt or soy sauces are added, sodium levels can become high, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed fish can be served as a main dish, added to salads, soups or grain bowls. It pairs well with lemon, fresh herbs, olive oil and light yogurt‑based sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw completely and re‑steam before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Pineapple juice, 100% is a pure juice extracted from ripe pineapples without added sugar, preservatives or flavorings. It has a bright sweet‑tart taste, characteristic tropical aroma and a rich golden colour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pineapple contains the enzyme bromelain, which helps break down proteins.
The fruit is cultivated in over 80 countries, with Costa Rica, the Philippines and Thailand being the largest producers.
Pineapple juice is often used in marinades because bromelain tenderises meat.
A single serving (250 ml) provides more than 100% of the daily recommended vitamin C.
In ancient cultures pineapple was a symbol of hospitality and luxury.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis and acts as a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: The bromelain enzyme improves digestion, reduces inflammation and may aid recovery after exercise.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B6 and folate contribute to energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Being almost 90% water, the juice helps maintain proper fluid balance.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal heart and muscle function and regulates fluid balance.

items.title: Bromelain allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bromelain, such as swelling, itching or hives.

items.title: High natural sugar content
items.content: Even without added sugar, the natural sugars can be a concern for people with diabetes or low‑carb diets.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature of the juice may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Interaction with medication
items.content: Bromelain can enhance the effect of anticoagulants, so consult a doctor if you are on blood‑thinning medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled as a refreshing beverage, add it to smoothies, cocktails, sauces and marinades. To reduce acidity, dilute with water or mix with mint.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 1 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 12 hours to prevent spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Sausage and peppers, no sauce is a dish made of sliced smoked or boiled sausage cooked together with sweet and hot peppers. It is served without tomato or cream sauces, so the main flavors come from the meat and aromatic spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originates from Italian cuisine, where sweet bell peppers and Italian sausage (salsiccia) are traditionally used.
Peppers add vitamin C and carotenoids, which enhance iron absorption from the meat.
It cooks quickly – about 10‑15 minutes over high heat.
Without sauce the dish is easier to control for calories and sugar content.
Sausage and peppers are often served as a side to pasta, rice, or potatoes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Sausage provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed, especially when paired with vitamin C from peppers.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sausage supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from peppers
items.content: Sweet and hot peppers are rich in carotenoids and vitamin C, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: The combination of protein and vitamins helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Some sausages are high in saturated fat, which should be limited in cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Peppers may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Many sausages use nitrites and other preservatives that can be harmful in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course, toss it with pasta, rice, couscous, or use it as a sandwich filling. Peppers can be cut into large chunks or thin strips according to personal preference.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Avoid freezing sausage with peppers if you plan to reheat, as the pepper texture may change.
